posts.topic: AGI and interest rates — why transformative AI could suppress rather than raise the cost of capital
posts.source_headline: AGI Could Lower Interest Rates
posts.x_post: The standard macro assumption about AGI gets the direction of interest rates exactly backwards. Every economist running a standard growth model concludes that expectations of transformative AI should push long-term rates higher — faster growth means more competition for capital, higher returns, higher discount rates. A new heterogeneous-agent asset pricing model shows the opposite can hold, and the mechanism matters enormously for how to price assets over the next decade. The key variable is wealth concentration. When AGI automates most human labor, the gains flow overwhelmingly to capital owners. Capital owners, almost by definition, have a much lower marginal propensity to consume than workers do. That surplus savings floods into financial markets rather than into goods markets. Aggregate demand for capital investment rises, but the supply of savings rises faster. The result: the real rate of return falls even as economic output accelerates sharply. This mirrors what happened during the early stages of the original Industrial Revolution, when productivity surged in specific sectors while the broader population experienced falling real wages, and bond yields in Britain compressed rather than exploded. The second-order consequence crushes the standard narrative that AI will force central banks into a tightening cycle. If AGI lands as a deflationary supply shock concentrated in the hands of asset owners, the Fed faces structurally low neutral rates, not a return to the 1970s. Duration assets and fixed income outperform in that world; commodity-linked inflation hedges underperform. Positioning for AGI as an inflationary event is the consensus trade. It may also be the wrong one.

posts.topic: AI chatbot legal liability and corporate accountability
posts.source_headline: Jake Moffatt's grandmother died in November 2022. He went online to book a flight to her funeral. Air Canada's chatbot told him there was a bereavement fare pro

The Air Canada chatbot case is the most important AI liability ruling most people filed under 'funny customer service story.' A British Columbia tribunal ruled in 2024 that Air Canada bore full responsibility for misinformation its chatbot gave Jake Moffatt about bereavement fares. Moffatt paid for a bereavement flight, the chatbot told him to apply for the discount within 90 days after travel, the real policy required application before departure. Air Canada lost and owed Moffatt $812.02 CAD plus fees.

The mechanism matters more than the outcome. Air Canada argued the chatbot was a 'separate legal entity' responsible for its own statements. The tribunal rejected that outright. A company deploying an automated system inherits every representation that system makes, regardless of whether a human reviewed it. The chatbot's error rate is irrelevant. The deployment decision is the liability trigger.

Now stack that principle against the current AI deployment wave. Enterprises are pushing customer-facing agents across insurance claims, loan applications, medical triage, and travel bookings. Every one of those agents will occasionally hallucinate a policy, misquote a rate, or invert a deadline, just as the Air Canada bot inverted Moffatt's. The legal exposure scales with deployment surface, and most legal teams have not caught up to that math. A $812 judgment becomes a class action the moment 4,000 users receive the same wrong instruction.

The Moffatt ruling redraws where accountability sits in the AI stack. The model vendor does not absorb it. The integration partner does not absorb it. The enterprise that deployed the agent absorbs it, fully, on the first wrong answer. Boards approving AI rollout plans in 2025 are approving liability schedules they have not yet priced.
